title: Strength training for endurance performance
goal: Judge how strongly heavy strength training improves endurance performance, durability and the sprint finish in running and cycling, and what limits the trials.

steps.title: Beyond economy: does performance improve?
steps.text:
The economy lesson showed that strength training lowers the oxygen cost of running by about 4%. But races are won on time, not on cost. Does performance follow?

A 2018 [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 28 studies in running, cycling, cross-country skiing and swimming found a moderate gain in middle- and long-distance performance ([effect size](g:effect-size) 0.52, 95% [CI](g:confidence-interval) 0.33–0.70), along with better energy cost, maximal force and maximal power. Training for maximal force, that is [heavy strength training](g:heavy-strength-training), gave bigger gains than lighter loads, and the benefit held at every performance level [[c:berryman]].

An earlier [systematic review](g:systematic-review) of 26 studies in trained endurance athletes agreed: strength training improved time-trial performance, economy and muscle power [[c:beattie]].

claims.text: Across 28 studies in four endurance sports, strength training moderately improved middle- and long-distance performance (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.33–0.70); maximal-force training gave the largest gains, at every performance level.

evidence.quote: The implementation of a strength-training mesocycle in running, cycling, cross-country skiing, and swimming was associated with moderate improvements in middle- and long-distance performance (net SMD [95%CI] = 0.52 [0.33-0.70]).
Maximal-force training led to greater improvements than other intensities. Subgroup analyses also revealed that beneficial effects on performance were consistent irrespective of the athletes' level.

claims.text: A systematic review of 26 studies found that strength training improved time-trial performance, economy and muscle power in competitive endurance athletes.

evidence.quote: The results showed that strength training improved time-trial performance, economy, [Formula: see text] and vMART in competitive endurance athletes.

steps.title: Running: heavy and mixed work help most
steps.text:
For runners, a 2024 meta-analysis compared methods on time-trial and time-to-exhaustion performance [[c:llanos-perf]]:

| method | effect on performance |
|---|---|
| heavy (≥80% of [1RM](g:one-rep-max)) | moderate (−0.47) |
| combined (two or more methods) | large (−1.04) |
| [plyometrics](g:plyometrics) | not significant (−0.21) |

Negative means faster. No method improved [VO2max](g:vo2max), the [maximal metabolic steady state](g:maximal-metabolic-steady-state) or sprint capacity. Certainty was moderate for heavy loads but very low for combined methods (6 studies, signs of publication bias).

A classic trial agrees: replacing 32% of training with explosive work (sprints, jumps) cut 5 km time in 10 trained athletes, through better economy and top running speed, with no change in VO₂max [[c:paavolainen]]. The gain comes from the muscles, not the heart.

claims.text: In middle- and long-distance runners, heavy and combined strength training improved running performance (moderate and large effects), plyometric training not significantly; no method improved VO₂max, vVO₂max, MMSS or sprint capacity. Certainty was moderate for heavy loads and very low for combined methods, where publication bias was found.

evidence.quote: High load and combined training methods induced moderate (effect size =  - 0.469, p = 0.029) and large effect (effect size =  - 1.035, p = 0.036) on running performance, respectively.
None of the training methods improved VO<sub>2</sub>max, vVO<sub>2</sub>max, MMSS, or sprint capacity (all p > 0.072).
The certainty of the evidence was very low to moderate.
Publication bias was found only in the analysis of running performance in the combined group

claims.text: Replacing 32% of training with explosive-strength training improved 5 km time, running economy and maximal anaerobic running speed in well-trained endurance athletes, without a change in VO₂max.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, the present simultaneous explosive-strength and endurance training improved the 5K time in well-trained endurance athletes without changes in their VO2 max.
This improvement was due to improved neuromuscular characteristics that were transferred into improved VMART and running economy.

steps.title: Cycling: more power, no extra weight
steps.text:
Most cycling trials come from one Norwegian group and one recipe: heavy strength training of four leg exercises, 3 sets of 4–10 [repetition maximum](g:repetition-maximum) (RM), twice a week.

- **20 well-trained cyclists, 12 weeks:** thigh [cross-sectional area](g:muscle-csa) and 40 min all-out power rose, with no rise in body mass [[c:ron10]].
- **19 trained women, 11 weeks:** better 40 min power, [fractional utilisation](g:fractional-utilisation) and economy; fewer [IIx](g:type-iix-fibre) and more [IIa](g:type-iia-fibre) fibres [[c:vik16]].
- **16 young elite cyclists, 25 weeks:** better 40 min power, but no change in VO₂max or economy [[c:ron15]].

An older review of 5 trials was less sure: the 3 with gains had replaced part of the riding with lifting, while the 2 without had added it on top [[c:yamamoto]].

claims.text: In well-trained cyclists, 12 weeks of heavy strength training increased thigh muscle CSA and 40 min all-out performance without increasing body mass.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, adding strength training to usual endurance training improved determinants of cycling performance as well as performance in well-trained cyclists. Of particular note is that the added strength training increased thigh muscle CSA without causing an increase in body mass.

claims.text: In female cyclists, 11 weeks of heavy strength training improved 40 min all-out power, fractional utilisation of VO₂max and cycling economy, with a shift from type IIAX-IIX toward IIA fibres.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, adding heavy strength training improved cycling performance, increased fractional utilization of VO2 max , and improved cycling economy.
The main mechanisms behind these improvements seemed to be increased quadriceps muscle CSA and fiber type shifts from type IIAX-IIX toward type IIA.

claims.text: In young elite cyclists, 25 weeks of heavy strength training improved 40 min all-out power without changes in VO₂max or cycling economy.

evidence.quote: Neither of the groups displayed alterations in VO2max or cycling economy.

claims.text: In a review of 5 trials in highly trained road cyclists, the 3 that improved performance replaced part of endurance training with resistance training; the 2 that added it on top found no improvement.

evidence.quote: Two of the 5 studies found no improvement in performance with CT, but these studies added RT on top of the athletes' existing ET. The 3 studies with improved cycling performance replaced a portion of the athletes' ET with RT

steps.title: Fresher legs late in long efforts
steps.text:
[Durability](g:durability) is how well you hold your power after hours of work. Two small trials tested whether strength training helps it.

In 20 well-trained cyclists, 12 weeks of heavy strength training raised mean power in a 5 min all-out effort done after 185 min of easy riding, from 371 to 400 W; the endurance-only group didn't change. In the last hour of the long ride, the strength group also used less oxygen, with lower heart rate, lactate and effort [[c:ron11]].

In 19 trained female duathletes, 11 weeks of the same recipe raised 5 min power after 3 h of cycling by 7.0%, and 5 min running performance after 1.5 h of running by 4.7% [[c:vik17]].

claims.text: In well-trained cyclists, adding 12 weeks of heavy strength training raised 5 min all-out power after 185 min of cycling from 371 to 400 W, and lowered oxygen uptake, heart rate, lactate and RPE in the last hour.

evidence.quote: Further, E+S increased the mean power output during the 5-min all-out trial (from 371 ± 9 to 400 ± 13 W, P<0.05), while no change occurred in E.
E+S led to greater reductions than E in oxygen consumption, heart rate, blood lactate concentration, and rate of perceived exertion (P<0.05) during the last hour of the prolonged cycling.

claims.text: In well-trained female duathletes, 11 weeks of heavy strength training improved 5 min all-out performance after prolonged work in both cycling (7.0%) and running (4.7%).

evidence.quote: Performance during the 5-min all-out test increased in both cycling (7.0 ± 4.5%) and running (4.7 ± 6.0%) in E+S, whereas no changes occurred in E

steps.title: Percentage change in power
steps.problem: After strength training, mean 5 min power after 185 min of riding rose from 371 to 400 W. What is the percentage change?
steps: Divide by the starting value, not the end value: 29 ÷ 371 = 0.078.
× 100 = 7.8%. Dividing by 400 instead gives 7.3%, a common slip.

steps.title: The sprint finish: plausible, not proven
steps.text:
Strength training should help a finishing kick, and some results agree. In cyclists, heavy strength training raised peak power in a 30 s [Wingate test](g:wingate-test) [[c:wingate]]. In runners, explosive training raised maximal 20 m speed [[c:v20]]. A 2018 review of 24 running studies judged that strength work tended to improve time trials and sprint qualities, though not in every study [[c:blagrove-sprint]].

But the 2024 running meta-analysis found that no method improved sprint capacity [[c:llanos-sprint]].

Part of the gap is what is measured: a fresh lab sprint is not a sprint at the end of a race, and the trials are small.

claims.text: In well-trained and elite cyclists, heavy strength training increased peak power in the 30 s Wingate test more than endurance training alone.

evidence.quote: E + S increased thigh muscle CSA, maximal isometric force, and peak power in the Wingate test more than E.
ES, but not E, resulted in increases in isometric half squat performance, lean lower body mass, peak power output during Wingate test

claims.text: Explosive-strength training increased maximal 20 m speed in well-trained endurance athletes, while it fell in controls.

evidence.quote: V20 m and 5J increased in E (P < 0.01) and decreased in C (P < 0.05).

claims.text: A systematic review of 24 running studies found good, but not consistent, evidence that strength training improves running economy, time trials and sprint performance.

evidence.quote: Whilst there was good evidence that ST improves RE, TT, and sprint performance, this was not a consistent finding across all works that were reviewed.

claims.text: In a 2024 meta-analysis of runners, no strength training method improved sprint capacity.

evidence.quote: None of the training methods improved VO<sub>2</sub>max, vVO<sub>2</sub>max, MMSS, or sprint capacity (all p > 0.072).

debate.question: Does strength training improve an endurance athlete's sprint finish?

sides.position: Yes: single trials show better Wingate peak power and short sprint speed, and a running review found sprint performance tended to improve.
Not clearly: pooled across runner trials, no method improved sprint capacity.

steps.title: Grading it honestly
steps.text:
Put together, strength training improving endurance performance is **moderate** evidence: several meta-analyses agree, but the trials beneath them are weak.

- **Small:** often 15–20 athletes, split into two groups.
- **Short:** 6–40 weeks in the running trials, 11–25 in the cycling ones above.
- **Fair quality:** the running review rated its studies 4–6 out of 10 on the [PEDro scale](g:pedro-scale) [[c:pedro]], and some cycling trials say 'assigned', not 'randomised'.
- **Unblinded:** athletes know they lift, and no [placebo](g:placebo) is possible.

One worry can go: in the running review, body composition was not harmed [[c:bodycomp]].

Grades: performance and economy moderate; durability weak; sprint finish disputed.

claims.text: In a systematic review of 24 strength training studies in distance runners, PEDro scores were 4–6 out of 10.

evidence.quote: PEDro scores revealed internal validity of 4, 5, or 6 for the studies reviewed.

claims.text: Strength training did not negatively affect body composition in distance runners.

evidence.quote: Importantly for the distance runner, measures relating to body composition are not negatively impacted by a ST intervention.

points: Strength training improves endurance performance, not only economy: a moderate effect across 28 studies in four sports, largest with heavy loads.
Runners: heavy and combined methods improved performance; plyometrics alone didn't reach significance. VO₂max doesn't change: the gain comes from the muscles.
Cyclists: heavy lifting (3 × 4–10 RM, twice a week) raised 40 min power and muscle size without raising body mass. Adding it on top of full riding worked less well in older trials.
Durability: two small trials found better 5 min power after hours of work (weak evidence).
Sprint finish: disputed. The trials are small, short, unblinded and rated fair at best.

variants.stem: Across 28 studies in four endurance sports, what did the 2018 meta-analysis find for strength training and performance?

options.text: A moderate gain, largest with maximal-force training, at every level
options.why: Right: SMD 0.52, with heavy (maximal-force) training best and the benefit consistent across performance levels.

options.text: A gain only in elite athletes, too small to matter for amateurs
options.why: The benefit was consistent irrespective of the athletes' level.

options.text: Better economy but no change in race performance
options.why: Performance improved too (SMD 0.52), together with energy cost, force and power.

options.text: A gain mainly from light, high-repetition circuits
options.why: Maximal-force (heavy) training led to greater improvements than other intensities.

variants.stem: A half-marathon runner has two gym slots a week for 12 weeks and wants the best chance of a faster race. Based on the 2024 meta-analysis of runners, which programme?

options.text: Heavy lifting combined with plyometrics
options.why: Right: combined methods gave the largest effect on performance (on very low-certainty evidence), and heavy lifting alone a moderate one; either way, heavy lifting is in it.

options.text: Plyometrics alone, since jumping is closest to running
options.why: Plyometric training alone didn't have a significant effect on performance in this analysis.

options.text: Light circuits at about 30% of 1RM, to avoid fatigue
options.why: Loads under 40% of 1RM counted as the control condition in this meta-analysis, not as a strength method.

options.text: None: strength work only changes VO₂max, which she can train by running
options.why: No method changed VO₂max; the performance gains came without it.

variants.stem: Explosive-strength training cut 5 km times in well-trained athletes without any change in their VO₂max. Which explanation fits the data best?

options.text: Their muscles got better: running economy and top running speed improved
options.why: Right: the 5 km gain tracked changes in economy and maximal anaerobic running speed, i.e. neuromuscular qualities.

options.text: VO₂max must have risen, but the test missed it
options.why: VO₂max was measured and didn't change in the explosive group; the explanation lies elsewhere.

options.text: They simply trained more hours than the control group
options.why: Total training volume was kept the same in both groups: part of the endurance training was replaced.

options.text: They lost body fat, so they carried less weight
options.why: Body fat isn't what the study linked to the gain; it tied the 5 km change to economy and maximal speed.

variants.stem: A climber-type road cyclist refuses heavy squats: 'bulk will cost me watts per kilo.' What did the 12-week trial in 20 well-trained cyclists find?

options.text: Thigh muscle grew, body mass didn't rise, and 40 min power improved
options.why: Right: the added strength training increased thigh CSA without increasing body mass, and 40 min all-out power rose.

options.text: Body mass rose by several kilos, cancelling out the power gain
options.why: The study specifically noted no increase in body mass.

options.text: Thigh muscle didn't change at all; only the nerves adapted
options.why: Thigh muscle CSA increased more in the strength group than in the endurance-only group.

options.text: Power rose, but power per kilo fell because of the extra muscle
options.why: With no rise in body mass, more power means more power per kilo, not less.

variants.stem: In the 11-week trial of female cyclists, which muscle changes went with better 40 min performance?

options.text: A bigger quadriceps, and a shift from IIx toward IIa fibres
options.why: Right: both the rise in quadriceps CSA and the IIAX-IIX to IIA shift correlated with the performance gain.

options.text: A shift from type IIa to type I fibres
options.why: The shift was from the fastest fibres (IIx) to IIa; type II to type I switches are rare, as the muscle module showed.

options.text: A smaller quadriceps, so less mass to carry
options.why: Quadriceps CSA increased, and a bigger increase went with a bigger performance gain.

options.text: A higher VO₂max from the lifting
options.why: The gains were in fractional utilisation and economy; the strength training isn't where VO₂max gains come from.

variants.stem: A 2010 review found that 2 of 5 trials of strength training in highly trained road cyclists showed no performance gain. What set those 2 apart, according to the review?

options.text: They added lifting on top of the usual riding instead of replacing some of it
options.why: Right: the 3 trials with gains replaced part of the endurance training with resistance training.

options.text: They used heavier loads than the trials that worked
options.why: The review didn't single out heavier loads; 2 of the positive trials used explosive-type exercises, and later trials show heavy loads work.

options.text: They tested women, who don't respond to strength training
options.why: The review didn't explain the split by sex, and later trials in women found clear gains.

options.text: They were done in the racing season, not the off-season
options.why: The review didn't explain the split by season; it pointed to adding versus replacing training.

variants.stem: A triathlete's mean 5 min power after a 3 h ride rises from 250 to 268 W after a winter of heavy lifting. What is the percentage change?

options.why: This divides by the end value (18 ÷ 268); percentage change uses the starting value.
18 is the change in watts, not a percentage.
A decimal slip: 0.072 × 100 = 7.2%, not 0.72%.

variants.stem: A runner covers 1,500 m in a 5 min all-out effort at the end of a 90 min run. After 11 weeks of heavy lifting, she covers 1,560 m. What is the percentage change?

options.why: This divides by the end value (60 ÷ 1,560); percentage change uses the starting value.
60 is the change in metres, not a percentage.
A decimal slip: 0.040 × 100 = 4.0%, not 0.4%.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 5 min power after a long ride rises from 320 to 344 W. What is the percentage change?

options.why: This divides by the end value (24 ÷ 344); percentage change uses the starting value.
24 is the change in watts, not a percentage.
A decimal slip: 0.075 × 100 = 7.5%, not 0.75%.

variants.stem: In the last hour of a 185 min ride at a fixed power, cyclists who had done strength training used less oxygen, with lower heart rate and lactate, than before. What does this point to?

options.text: Better economy: the same power cost less late on
options.why: Right: same power, less oxygen. A proposed reason is that stronger fibres delay the call-up of less efficient type II fibres as fatigue builds.

options.text: Their VO₂max had risen, so they had more headroom
options.why: VO₂max is the maximum; using less oxygen at a fixed submaximal power is about economy, not the ceiling.

options.text: They rode more slowly during the final hour
options.why: The ride was at a fixed power (44% of maximal aerobic power), so they weren't slower.

options.text: Their hearts had grown bigger from lifting
options.why: Heart size wasn't measured, and the oxygen saving points to the muscles, not to the heart.

variants.stem: A coach sells heavy lifting to triathletes as 'proven to give you a sprint finish'. How should you grade that claim?

options.text: Disputed: small trials show better lab sprints, but a meta-analysis found no effect
options.why: Right: Wingate and 20 m speed gains come from single small trials, while pooled runner data found no improvement in sprint capacity.

options.text: Strong: every trial agrees that sprint power rises
options.why: Not every trial agrees: the running review called it inconsistent, and the 2024 meta-analysis found no effect.

options.text: Disproven: lifting makes muscles slower
options.why: No trial showed slower sprints; some showed faster ones. The evidence is mixed, not negative.

options.text: Strong, because stronger muscles always sprint faster
options.why: That is a mechanism argument; it doesn't replace trial evidence, which is mixed here.

variants.stem: The 185 min cycling trial 'assigned' 11 men to strength training and 9 riders (7 men, 2 women) to endurance only. What most weakens it as proof of cause and effect?

options.text: Small groups, not clearly randomised, that differed in make-up
options.why: Right: with about 10 per group, no stated random allocation and different groups, chance or group differences could explain part of the result.

options.text: A 5 min effort is too short to say anything about endurance
options.why: The 5 min effort came after 185 min of riding: it was designed to test performance under fatigue.

options.text: Twelve weeks is too long for strength gains to last
options.why: Twelve weeks is a normal training study length; 1RM rose clearly by the end.

options.text: Power is less reliable to measure than oxygen uptake
options.why: Power on a lab ergometer is measured precisely; measurement isn't the main weakness here.
